newsitem.title: USA: Ford CEO Trotman agrees to stay until 2000.
newsitem.headline: Ford CEO Trotman agrees to stay until 2000.

text.p: Ford Motor Co said Thursday that Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Alex Trotman accepted a board request to remain in his post until January 1, 2000.
"In making the request, the board said it was very supportive of Trotman and the entire Ford management team and the direction in which it is leading the company," Ford said in a statement.
The board also believes the "major changes" being made to Ford's operating processes would benefit from continuing stability of its management team, the company said.

The company launched an aggressive restructuring program called Ford 2000 in January 1995 under Trotman to streamline the automaker's product development system. Some analysts have voiced skepticism the ambitious cost-cutting plan can reach all of its goals.
The board request for Trotman to stay on came after its normal annual performance review of the CEO, Ford said.

The board action means Trotman, 63, will be able to stay on past his 65th birthday in July 1998, the customary retirement age for senior Ford executives. Trotman was elected chairman November 1, 1993.
Ford spokeswoman Pam Kueber said the company does not require executives to leave at age 65, noting that former Chairman Harold "Red" Poling stayed until he was 68.
Last September a published report said the board had asked Trotman to remain as chairman and CEO, bypassing Edward Hagenlocker.
The report also said William Clay Ford Jr, a board member and Ford family member, was a candidate to become the company's next chairman.
Hagenlocker, who had been president of Ford's Automotive Operations, was named vice chairman October 10, 1996.
Ford denied the report and later issued a statement saying no decisions had been made on Trotman's successor.
Kueber said today the board made no other executive changes.
"Everything else remains the same," she said.
She declined to speculate on future board actions.
